claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the etiological agent of tuberculosis.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiological agent of tuberculosis, devotes a considerable amount of coding capacity to produce, sense, and degrade cAMP.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the causative agent of tuberculosis.

claim: Mtb devotes a considerable amount of coding capacity to produce, sense, and degrade cAMP.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the etiological agent of tuberculosis, devotes a considerable amount of coding capacity to produce, sense, and degrade cAMP.
evidence: This is supported by the genomic analysis showing multiple adenylate cyclases, phosphodiesterases, and cAMP-binding proteins encoded in the Mtb genome.

claim: Rv3645 is the sole essential adenylate cyclase in Mtb H37Rv.
source: Here, we took a genetic approach to investigate the function of the sole essential adenylate cyclase in Mtb H37Rv, Rv3645.
evidence: This is supported by prior essentiality screens and the experimental data showing rv3645 is essential under standard laboratory conditions.

claim: A lack of rv3645 results in increased sensitivity to numerous antibiotics.
source: We found that a lack of rv3645 resulted in increased sensitivity to numerous antibiotics by a mechanism independent of substantial increases in envelope permeability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CRISPRi screening data and MIC assays shown in Figure 1.

claim: The increased antibiotic sensitivity caused by lack of rv3645 is independent of substantial increases in envelope permeability.
source: We found that a lack of rv3645 resulted in increased sensitivity to numerous antibiotics by a mechanism independent of substantial increases in envelope permeability.
evidence: This is supported by the drug uptake assays and permeability measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: rv3645 is conditionally essential for Mtb growth only in the presence of long-chain fatty acids.
source: We made the unexpected observation that rv3645 is conditionally essential for Mtb growth only in the presence of long-chain fatty acids, a host-relevant carbon source.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth experiments showing Δrv3645 can grow in fatty acid-free media but not in the presence of oleic acid (Figure 3).

claim: Mutations in the atypical cAMP phosphodiesterase rv1339 suppress both fatty acid and drug sensitivity phenotypes in strains lacking rv3645.
source: A suppressor screen further identified mutations in the atypical cAMP phosphodiesterase rv1339 that suppress both fatty acid and drug sensitivity phenotypes in strains lacking rv3645.
evidence: This is supported by the CRISPRi suppressor screen and spontaneous suppressor isolation experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Rv3645 is the dominant source of cAMP under standard laboratory growth conditions.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we found that Rv3645 is the dominant source of cAMP under standard laboratory growth conditions, that cAMP production is the essential function of Rv3645 in the presence of long-chain fatty acids, and that reduced cAMP levels result in increased long-chain fatty acid uptake and metabolism and increased antibiotic susceptibility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry measurements showing a 31-fold reduction in cAMP in the rv3645 deletion strain (Figure 5C).

claim: cAMP production is the essential function of Rv3645 in the presence of long-chain fatty acids.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we found that Rv3645 is the dominant source of cAMP under standard laboratory growth conditions, that cAMP production is the essential function of Rv3645 in the presence of long-chain fatty acids, and that reduced cAMP levels result in increased long-chain fatty acid uptake and metabolism and increased antibiotic susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by the inability of the adenylate cyclase catalytic mutant to complement the fatty acid sensitivity phenotype (Figure 5A).

claim: Reduced cAMP levels result in increased long-chain fatty acid uptake and metabolism.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we found that Rv3645 is the dominant source of cAMP under standard laboratory growth conditions, that cAMP production is the essential function of Rv3645 in the presence of long-chain fatty acids, and that reduced cAMP levels result in increased long-chain fatty acid uptake and metabolism and increased antibiotic susceptibility.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the [1-14C]-oleic acid uptake and metabolism experiments shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Reduced cAMP levels result in increased antibiotic susceptibility.
source: Using mass spectrometry, we found that Rv3645 is the dominant source of cAMP under standard laboratory growth conditions, that cAMP production is the essential function of Rv3645 in the presence of long-chain fatty acids, and that reduced cAMP levels result in increased long-chain fatty acid uptake and metabolism and increased antibiotic susceptibility.
evidence: This is supported by the MIC assays showing increased drug sensitivity in rv3645 knockdown strains and rv1339 overexpression strains (Figures 1 and 5).

claim: Hypoxia reduces Mtb respiratory capacity and activates the DosRST two-component system.
source: For example, hypoxia reduces Mtb respiratory capacity and activates the DosRST two-component system (Park et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Park et al., 2003.

claim: DosR induces a 48 gene regulon which ultimately slows growth, promoting survival under hypoxic conditions and tolerance to antibiotics that are more active against rapidly replicating bacteria.
source: DosR induces a 48 gene regulon which ultimately slows growth, promoting survival under hypoxic conditions and tolerance to antibiotics that are more active against rapidly replicating bacteria (Galagan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Galagan et al., 2013.

claim: Nutrient starvation results in the dephosphorylation of CwlM, a substrate of the eukaryotic-like protein serine/threonine kinase PknB.
source: In a second example, nutrient starvation results in the dephosphorylation of CwlM, a substrate of the eukaryotic-like protein serine/threonine kinase PknB (Boutte et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Boutte et al., 2016.

claim: Dephosphorylation of CwlM reduces CwlM interaction with and activation of the peptidoglycan biosynthetic enzyme MurA, thereby reducing cell wall metabolism and promoting tolerance to starvation and antibiotics.
source: Dephosphorylation reduces CwlM interaction with and activation of the peptidoglycan biosynthetic enzyme MurA, thereby reducing cell wall metabolism and promoting tolerance to starvation and antibiotics.
evidence: This is based on the mechanistic understanding of CwlM function cited from Boutte et al., 2016.

claim: E. coli encodes only one adenylate cyclase.
source: Whereas the model bacteria E. coli encodes only one adenylate cyclase, the adenylate cyclase gene family has undergone a remarkable expansion in mycobacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli adenylate cyclase.

claim: M. avium encodes 12 predicted adenylate cyclases.
source: M. avium, M. marinum, and Mtb encode 12, 31, and at least 15 predicted adenylate cyclases (Shenoy and Visweswariah, 2006), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shenoy and Visweswariah, 2006.

claim: M. marinum encodes 31 predicted adenylate cyclases.
source: M. avium, M. marinum, and Mtb encode 12, 31, and at least 15 predicted adenylate cyclases (Shenoy and Visweswariah, 2006), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shenoy and Visweswariah, 2006.

claim: Mtb encodes at least 15 predicted adenylate cyclases.
source: M. avium, M. marinum, and Mtb encode 12, 31, and at least 15 predicted adenylate cyclases (Shenoy and Visweswariah, 2006), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shenoy and Visweswariah, 2006 and confirmed by the genomic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mtb adenylate cyclases can be activated by pH.
source: Mtb adenylate cyclases can be activated by a variety of stimuli, including pH (Tews et al., 2005), bicarbonate (Cann et al., 2003), and fatty acids (Abdel Motaal et al., 2006), with the resulting increase in cAMP levels modulating both bacterial and host physiology (Agarwal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tews et al., 2005.

claim: Mtb adenylate cyclases can be activated by bicarbonate.
source: Mtb adenylate cyclases can be activated by a variety of stimuli, including pH (Tews et al., 2005), bicarbonate (Cann et al., 2003), and fatty acids (Abdel Motaal et al., 2006), with the resulting increase in cAMP levels modulating both bacterial and host physiology (Agarwal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cann et al., 2003.

claim: Mtb adenylate cyclases can be activated by fatty acids.
source: Mtb adenylate cyclases can be activated by a variety of stimuli, including pH (Tews et al., 2005), bicarbonate (Cann et al., 2003), and fatty acids (Abdel Motaal et al., 2006), with the resulting increase in cAMP levels modulating both bacterial and host physiology (Agarwal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abdel Motaal et al., 2006.

claim: Nearly 1% of the Mtb genome is predicted to produce, degrade, or interact with cAMP.
source: This expansion of the adenylate cyclase gene family is mirrored by an expansion of predicted cAMP phosphodiesterases, effectors, and binding proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) – nearly 1% of the Mtb genome is predicted to produce, degrade, or interact with cAMP.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and annotation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of rv3645 sensitized Mtb to numerous antibiotics with unrelated mechanisms of action.
source: Amongst the non-target hit genes, we found that depletion of the predicted essential adenylate cyclase, rv3645 (Figure 1A), sensitized Mtb to numerous antibiotics with unrelated mechanisms of action (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CRISPRi screening data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: rv3645 was the only adenylate cyclase whose knockdown resulted in increased drug sensitivity under standard laboratory culture conditions.
source: Interestingly, rv3645 was the only adenylate cyclase whose knockdown resulted in increased drug sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating a lack of substantial functional redundancy for adenylate cyclases under these culture conditions.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the CRISPRi screening data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a lack of substantial functional redundancy for adenylate cyclases under standard laboratory culture conditions.
source: Interestingly, rv3645 was the only adenylate cyclase whose knockdown resulted in increased drug sensitivity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), demonstrating a lack of substantial functional redundancy for adenylate cyclases under these culture conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only rv3645 knockdown resulted in drug sensitivity among all adenylate cyclases tested.

claim: Knockdown of rv3645 prevented growth on 7H10-OADC agar plates.
source: Consistent with prior screens (Bosch et al., 2021; DeJesus et al., 2017), knockdown of rv3645 prevented growth on 7H10-OADC agar plates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 1C and supported by citations to prior screens.

claim: The growth defect caused by rv3645 knockdown was complemented by expressing a CRISPRi-resistant but not a CRISPRi-sensitive rv3645 allele.
source: This growth defect was complemented by expressing a CRISPRi-resistant but not a CRISPRi-sensitive rv3645 allele, demonstrating that growth inhibition was indeed a result of silencing rv3645.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the complementation experiments shown in Figure 1C.

claim: rv3645 knockdown sensitized Mtb to vancomycin, rifampicin, clarithromycin, bedaquiline, and meropenem.
source: Consistent with the CRISPRi screening results, rv3645 knockdown sensitized Mtb to vancomycin, rifampicin, clarithromycin, bedaquiline, and meropenem but not other drugs (Figure 1D–G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assays shown in Figures 1D-G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-H.

claim: rv3645 knockdown did not sensitize Mtb to isoniazid, ethambutol, or levofloxacin.
source: Consistent with the CRISPRi screening results, rv3645 knockdown sensitized Mtb to vancomycin, rifampicin, clarithromycin, bedaquiline, and meropenem but not other drugs (Figure 1D–G; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-H.

claim: The chemical-genetic signatures of rv3645 and envelope biosynthetic genes are similar.
source: The similarities between the chemical-genetic signatures of rv3645 and envelope biosynthetic genes (Figure 2A; Li et al., 2022) suggested that rv3645 may contribute to intrinsic drug resistance by promoting envelope integrity in Mtb.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the screening profiles shown in Figure 2A.

claim: rv3645 knockdown strains showed only a modest increase in BODIPY-VAN uptake compared to the positive control gene mtrA.
source: Surprisingly, despite the dramatic sensitization of rv3645 knockdown strains to vancomycin (Figure 1D), rv3645 knockdown strains showed only a modest increase in BODIPY-VAN uptake (Figure 2B) as compared to the positive control gene mtrA, encoding a two-component response regulator important for proper envelope biogenesis (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the BODIPY-VAN uptake assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: BODIPY-VAN retained similar antimicrobial activity to vancomycin.
source: To ensure the discrepancy between rv3645 MIC assays and drug uptake measurements was not due to the presence of the BODIPY conjugate (~274 Daltons), we first confirmed that BODIPY-VAN retained similar antimicrobial activity to vancomycin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dose-response curves shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No loss in colony forming units occurred when treating the panel of Mtb strains with vancomycin for the same time scale as the uptake assay.
source: To ensure that the BODIPY-VAN uptake assay was not confounded by differential cell death and lysis (cells which presumably would not stain with BODIPY-VAN), we confirmed that no loss in colony forming units (CFU) occurred when treating this panel of Mtb strains with vancomycin for the same time scale as the uptake assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the time-kill curves shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: rv3645 knockdown strains did not show elevated levels of vancomycin uptake by mass spectrometry.
source: Consistent with the BODIPY-VAN results, rv3645 knockdown strains did not show elevated levels of vancomycin uptake (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: rv3645 knockdown strains were not hyperpermeable to ethidium bromide, calcein-AM, and BCECF-AM compared to positive control genes involved in envelope biosynthesis and integrity.
source: Finally, we monitored envelope permeability with the reporter dyes ethidium bromide, calcein-AM, and BCECF-AM. As with the vancomycin uptake assays, rv3645 knockdown strains were not hyperpermeable to these dyes, as compared to the positive control genes involved in envelope biosynthesis and integrity (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dye uptake assays shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Depletion of rv3645 does not result in large increases in Mtb envelope permeability.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that depletion of rv3645 does not result in large increases in Mtb envelope permeability.
evidence: This is concluded from the multiple permeability assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Rv3645-mediated intrinsic drug resistance occurs primarily by a mechanism other than increasing envelope permeability.
source: Thus, Rv3645-mediated intrinsic drug resistance must occur primarily by some other mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that drug sensitivity is not explained by increased envelope permeability.

claim: rv3645 knockdown no longer inhibited growth when the growth medium was supplemented without fatty acid (ADC) instead of with oleic acid (OADC).
source: Curiously, when the same growth medium was instead supplemented without fatty acid (ADC), rv3645 knockdown no longer inhibited growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that rv3645 is conditionally essential in the presence of oleic acid.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Δrv3645 is uniquely sensitive to long-chain fatty acids palmitic acid (C16:0), oleic acid (C18:1), and arachidonic acid (C20:4).
source: Δrv3645 was uniquely sensitive to long-chain fatty acids palmitic acid (C16:0), oleic acid (C18:1), and arachidonic acid (C20:4); but not too short or medium-chain fatty acids or cholesterol (Figure 3B–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fatty acid sensitivity assays shown in Figures 3B-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-G.

claim: Δrv3645 is not sensitive to short or medium-chain fatty acids or cholesterol.
source: Δrv3645 was uniquely sensitive to long-chain fatty acids palmitic acid (C16:0), oleic acid (C18:1), and arachidonic acid (C20:4); but not too short or medium-chain fatty acids or cholesterol (Figure 3B–D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the fatty acid sensitivity assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-G.

claim: Long-chain fatty acids are toxic to Δrv3645, rather than Δrv3645 being unable to consume them.
source: The fact that the growth of Δrv3645 in the presence of long-chain fatty acids was not rescued by alternative carbon sources in the medium (glycerol and glucose) suggests that long-chain fatty acids are toxic to Δrv3645, rather than Δrv3645 being unable to consume them.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that alternative carbon sources do not rescue growth in the presence of fatty acids.

claim: Δrv3645 showed elevated uptake and metabolism of [1-14C]-oleic acid.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, Δrv3645 showed elevated uptake and metabolism of [1-14C]-oleic acid (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the radioactive oleic acid uptake and metabolism assays shown in Figures 3E and F.

claim: The contribution of rv3645 to intrinsic drug resistance is dependent on the presence of long-chain fatty acids in the growth media.
source: As with the growth defect, drug sensitivity associated with Δrv3645 was also dependent on the presence of long-chain fatty acids in the growth media (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assays comparing growth in OADC vs ADC media shown in Figures 3G-I.

claim: The CRISPRi suppressor screen identified nine enriched genes, eight of which encode structural or catalytic subunits of the Mce1 transporter.
source: The suppressor screen identified nine enriched genes, eight of which encode structural or catalytic subunits of the Mce1 transporter (Figure 4B, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the suppressor screen results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mce1 has been shown to be an importer of fatty acids, including palmitic acid, in Mtb.
source: Mce1 has recently been shown to be an importer of fatty acids, including palmitic acid, in Mtb (Nazarova et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: The fatty acid toxicity phenotype of Δrv3645 is dependent on palmitic acid uptake and metabolism.
source: The fact that knockdown of the Mce1 transporter allows Δrv3645 to grow in the presence of palmitic acid suggests that the fatty acid toxicity phenotype of Δrv3645 is dependent on palmitic acid uptake and metabolism, consistent with recent results (Fieweger et al., 2023), rather than an uptake-independent toxicity mechanism such as fatty acid-dependent disruption of the Mtb envelope (Kengmo Tchoupa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the suppressor screen results and supported by citations to Fieweger et al., 2023 and Kengmo Tchoupa et al., 2022.

claim: rv1339 was the top hit in the CRISPRi suppressor screen.
source: The top hit in the CRISPRi suppressor screen was the non-essential gene rv1339 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the suppressor screen results shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Isolation of spontaneous suppressors of Δrv3645 grown in the presence of oleic acid identified five unique mutations in rv1339, including one frameshift mutation.
source: Consistent with the loss of Rv1339 activity suppressing the fatty acid sensitive phenotype of an Δrv3645 strain, isolation of spontaneous suppressors of Δrv3645 grown in the presence of oleic acid identified five unique mutations in rv1339, including one frameshift mutation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the whole genome sequencing of spontaneous suppressors shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CRISPRi knockdown of rv1339 rescued Δrv3645 fatty acid sensitivity.
source: We confirmed that CRISPRi knockdown of rv1339 rescued Δrv3645 fatty acid sensitivity with individual strains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the growth assay shown in Figure 4D.

claim: rv1339 knockdown rescued the vancomycin sensitivity phenotype of the Δrv3645 strain.
source: rv1339 knockdown rescued the vancomycin sensitivity phenotype of the Δrv3645 strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assay shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Rv1339 was recently reported to be an atypical cAMP phosphodiesterase.
source: Intriguingly, Rv1339 was recently reported to be an atypical cAMP phosphodiesterase (Thomson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thomson et al., 2022.

claim: The Rv3645 adenylate cyclase catalytic mutant was unable to complement oleic acid and vancomycin sensitivity phenotypes.
source: The Rv3645 adenylate cyclase catalytic mutant was unable to complement oleic acid and vancomycin sensitivity phenotypes (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the complementation experiments shown in Figures 5A and B.

claim: The catalytic mutant expressed at wild-type levels.
source: We confirmed by western blot that the catalytic mutant expressed at wild-type levels, and thus we attribute the lack of complementation specifically to the loss of cAMP synthesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the western blot shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 31-fold reduction in cAMP was observed in the rv3645 deletion strain.
source: A 31-fold reduction in cAMP was observed in the rv3645 deletion strain (Figure 5C) that could be rescued by the knockdown of rv1339 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The reduction in cAMP in the rv3645 deletion strain could be rescued by the knockdown of rv1339.
source: A 31-fold reduction in cAMP was observed in the rv3645 deletion strain (Figure 5C) that could be rescued by the knockdown of rv1339 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Overexpression of rv1339 in an otherwise wild-type background led to an 11-fold reduction in cAMP levels.
source: Conversely, overexpression of rv1339 in an otherwise wild-type background led to an 11-fold reduction in cAMP levels (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Overexpression of a catalytically dead rv1339 allele did not reduce cAMP levels.
source: Overexpression of a catalytically dead rv1339 allele did not reduce cAMP levels (Figure 5E; Thomson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 5E and supported by citation to Thomson et al., 2022.

claim: Reduction in cAMP levels in Δrv3645 and rv1339 overexpressing strains did not alter levels of ATP nor pyrophosphate.
source: Reduction in cAMP levels in Δrv3645 and rv1339 overexpressing strains did not alter levels of ATP nor pyrophosphate, involved in cAMP biosynthesis, indicating that the observed phenotypes are not caused by alterations in these metabolites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mass spectrometry measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overexpression of rv1339 resulted in elevated oleic acid uptake and metabolism.
source: Consistent with the role of cAMP in regulating long-chain fatty acid metabolism and drug sensitivity, overexpression of rv1339 resulted in elevated oleic acid uptake and metabolism and increased vancomycin sensitivity (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the oleic acid uptake and metabolism assays shown in Figures 5F and G.

claim: Overexpression of rv1339 resulted in increased vancomycin sensitivity.
source: Consistent with the role of cAMP in regulating long-chain fatty acid metabolism and drug sensitivity, overexpression of rv1339 resulted in elevated oleic acid uptake and metabolism and increased vancomycin sensitivity (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assay shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Elevated oleic acid uptake and metabolism were not mediated by changes in Mce1 protein expression levels.
source: Elevated oleic acid uptake and metabolism were not mediated by changes in Mce1 protein expression levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the western blot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Addition of V-59 rescued the vancomycin sensitivity of Δrv3645.
source: Addition of V-59 rescued the vancomycin sensitivity of Δrv3645 (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assay shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The addition of oleic acid did not alter cAMP levels as compared to fatty-acid-free media.
source: The addition of oleic acid did not alter cAMP levels as compared to fatty-acid-free media (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The presence of antibiotics variably increased cAMP levels.
source: While the presence of antibiotics variably increased cAMP levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B), there was no correlation between the drugs that result in elevated cAMP levels and those drugs that rv3645-KD is sensitized to (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ELISA measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B.

claim: There was no correlation between the drugs that result in elevated cAMP levels and those drugs that rv3645-KD is sensitized to.
source: While the presence of antibiotics variably increased cAMP levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 5B), there was no correlation between the drugs that result in elevated cAMP levels and those drugs that rv3645-KD is sensitized to (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 5B with Figure 1B-D.

claim: Rv3645 is not a detector of long-chain fatty acids or antibiotics.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Rv3645 is not a detector of long-chain fatty acids or antibiotics, but rather that cAMP produced by Rv3645 puts the bacilli in a physiologic state capable of surviving these stresses.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cAMP levels do not change in response to fatty acids or antibiotics.

claim: cAMP produced by Rv3645 puts the bacilli in a physiologic state capable of surviving long-chain fatty acids and antibiotics.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Rv3645 is not a detector of long-chain fatty acids or antibiotics, but rather that cAMP produced by Rv3645 puts the bacilli in a physiologic state capable of surviving these stresses.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and biochemical data showing that cAMP levels regulate fatty acid metabolism and drug sensitivity.

claim: rv3645 was not essential for in vitro growth in standard lab culture conditions in the lineage 2 strain HN878.
source: Unlike H37Rv, rv3645 was not essential for in vitro growth in standard lab culture conditions, consistent with prior screening results (Bosch et al., 2021; Carey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to prior screening results.

claim: The reduction of cAMP levels sensitized HN878 to both vancomycin and palmitic acid.
source: Despite this difference in essentiality, the reduction of cAMP levels sensitized HN878 to both vancomycin and palmitic acid (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC and growth assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: cAMP plays a critical role in regulating fatty acid metabolism and intrinsic drug resistance in Mtb.
source: Taken together, these data are consistent with a critical role for cAMP in regulating fatty acid metabolism and intrinsic drug resistance in Mtb.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive genetic and biochemical data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: MacE is predicted to be composed of six transmembrane helices and cytosolic HAMP and cyclase homology domains.
source: MacE is predicted to be composed of six transmembrane helices and cytosolic HAMP and cyclase homology domains.
evidence: This is based on domain prediction analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The presence of a HAMP domain suggests that MacE senses a ligand and transduces this signal into cytoplasmic cAMP production.
source: The presence of a HAMP domain, which typically transmits conformational changes from a periplasmic or transmembrane ligand binding domain to a cytoplasmic signaling domain (Hulko et al., 2006), suggests that MacE senses a ligand and transduces this signal into cytoplasmic cAMP production.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of HAMP domains cited from Hulko et al., 2006.

claim: Prior work established a link between cAMP and fatty acid catabolism through the cAMP-activated lysine acetyltransferase Mt-Pat.
source: Prior work established a link between cAMP and fatty acid catabolism through the cAMP-activated lysine acetyltransferase Mt-Pat (Nambi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nambi et al., 2013.

claim: Activated Mt-Pat acetylates/propionylates multiple enzymes involved in fatty acid catabolism, including ten FadD paralogs and acetyl-CoA synthetase, thereby inhibiting AMP-ligase activity and oxidation of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA.
source: Activated Mt-Pat acetylates/propionylates multiple enzymes involved in fatty acid catabolism, including ten FadD paralogs and acetyl-CoA synthetase, thereby inhibiting AMP-ligase activity and oxidation of fatty acids to acetyl-CoA.
evidence: This is based on prior work on Mt-Pat function cited from Nambi et al., 2013.

claim: Inactivation of Mt-Pat makes Mtb more sensitive to fatty acids.
source: Inactivation of Mt-Pat, like macE, makes Mtb more sensitive to fatty acids (Nambi et al., 2013; Rittershaus et al., 2018), although the fatty acid sensitivity phenotype is more severe for loss of macE as evidenced by the non-essentiality of Mt-Pat under standard laboratory culture conditions (DeJesus et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nambi et al., 2013, Rittershaus et al., 2018, and DeJesus et al., 2017.

claim: The fatty acid sensitivity phenotype is more severe for loss of macE than for loss of Mt-Pat.
source: Inactivation of Mt-Pat, like macE, makes Mtb more sensitive to fatty acids (Nambi et al., 2013; Rittershaus et al., 2018), although the fatty acid sensitivity phenotype is more severe for loss of macE as evidenced by the non-essentiality of Mt-Pat under standard laboratory culture conditions (DeJesus et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the essentiality of macE but not Mt-Pat under standard conditions.

claim: Transposon mutants in rv1339 showed reduced uptake of BODIPY-palmitate in infected macrophages.
source: Further linking cAMP and fatty acid metabolism, VanderVen and colleagues showed that transposon mutants in rv1339 showed reduced uptake of BODIPY-palmitate in infected macrophages (Nazarova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2019.

claim: Reduced cAMP levels lead to overactive fatty acid catabolism.
source: Collectively, growing evidence suggests that reduced cAMP levels lead to overactive fatty acid catabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective evidence presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: Mt-Pat mutants are strongly attenuated under hypoxia.
source: In a series of related findings, Sassetti and colleagues screened Mtb transposon mutant libraries and identified Mt-Pat mutants as strongly attenuated under hypoxia (Rittershaus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rittershaus et al., 2018.

claim: In the absence of Mt-Pat, Mtb fails to downregulate fatty acid catabolism under hypoxic conditions, leading to a continual flux of acetyl-CoA through oxidative TCA metabolism.
source: In the absence of Mt-Pat, it was hypothesized that Mtb fails to downregulate fatty acid catabolism under hypoxic conditions, leading to a continual flux of acetyl-CoA through oxidative TCA metabolism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the work cited from Rittershaus et al., 2018.

claim: Transposon mutants in the Mce1 transporter promoted fitness in hypoxia.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, the same screen identified that transposon mutants in the Mce1 transporter promoted fitness in hypoxia.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rittershaus et al., 2018.

claim: Under hypoxia, the TCA cycle is thought to preferentially work in the reductive direction to regenerate NAD and prevent the accumulation of NADH in the absence of a terminal electron acceptor.
source: Under hypoxia, the TCA cycle is thought to preferentially work in the reductive direction to regenerate NAD and prevent the accumulation of NADH in the absence of a terminal electron acceptor (Eoh and Rhee, 2013; Watanabe et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eoh and Rhee, 2013 and Watanabe et al., 2011.

claim: Δmt-pat under hypoxic conditions becomes redox imbalanced and depletes NAD.
source: As both the oxidative branch of the TCA cycle and fatty acid β-oxidation produce NADH, Δmt-pat under hypoxic conditions becomes redox imbalanced and depletes NAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic consequences of continued fatty acid catabolism under hypoxia.

claim: rv1339 is the top resistance-promoting hit in the hypoxia TnSeq data.
source: Also potentially consistent with this interpretation, re-analysis of the hypoxia TnSeq data identifies rv1339 as the top resistance-promoting hit (Rittershaus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on re-analysis of data from Rittershaus et al., 2018.

claim: Elevated cAMP levels in rv1339 transposon mutants could augment Mt-Pat activity and reduce fatty acid uptake and catabolism.
source: Elevated cAMP levels in rv1339 transposon mutants could augment Mt-Pat activity and reduce fatty acid uptake and catabolism and drive expression of malate dehydrogenase (Gazdik and McDonough, 2005), an enzyme critical for the reductive TCA cycle under hypoxia (Rittershaus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known functions of cAMP and Mt-Pat.

claim: Isolation of spontaneous resistant mutants to a series of novel inhibitors of the QcrB subunit of the cytochrome bc1-aa3 oxidase repeatedly identifies mutations in rv1339.
source: Finally, recent observations suggest a link between cAMP and the electron transport chain. Isolation of spontaneous resistant mutants to a series of novel inhibitors of the QcrB subunit of the cytochrome bc1-aa3 oxidase repeatedly identifies mutations in rv1339 (Chandrasekera et al., 2017; O'Malley et al., 2018; Shelton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chandrasekera et al., 2017, O'Malley et al., 2018, and Shelton et al., 2021.

claim: ΔmacE shows hypersensitivity to the QcrB inhibitor Q203.
source: Indeed, ΔmacE shows hypersensitivity to the QcrB inhibitor Q203 (Figure 5—figure supplement 7), potentially suggesting a cytochrome bd defect in this strain.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MIC assay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: Loss of macE reduces cAMP levels which reduces the activity of multiple cAMP effectors, including Mt-Pat.
source: Collectively, ours and published results lead to the following working model (Figure 5J). Loss of macE reduces cAMP levels which reduces the activity of multiple cAMP effectors, including Mt-Pat.
evidence: This is a model based on the collective data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No single annotated or predicted cAMP effector individually recapitulates the phenotypes observed with macE.
source: That no single annotated or predicted cAMP effector individually recapitulates the phenotypes observed with macE indicates that the physiological effects of reduced cAMP levels in ΔmacE are the consequence of the altered activity of multiple effectors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the screening data showing that no single effector knockdown phenocopies macE.

claim: Potential downstream cAMP effector proteins include transcription factors like CRP, transporters, phospholipases, and others.
source: Potential downstream cAMP effector proteins include transcription factors like CRP, transporters, phospholipases, and others (Johnson and McDonough, 2018), highlighting the potential pleiotropic consequences of modulating cAMP levels.
evidence: This is based on known cAMP effectors cited from Johnson and McDonough, 2018.

claim: Reduced activity of cAMP-responsive proteins may increase fatty acid uptake and catabolism and oxidative TCA metabolism while simultaneously reducing electron transport chain activity.
source: Reduced activity of cAMP-responsive proteins, including Mt-Pat, may increase fatty acid uptake and catabolism (Nazarova et al., 2019) and oxidative TCA metabolism while simultaneously reducing electron transport chain activity (Ko and Oh, 2020).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and cited literature.

claim: The derangement caused by reduced cAMP may ultimately lead to redox imbalance, perturbed membrane potential, reduced growth, and increased sensitivity to antibiotics.
source: This derangement may ultimately lead to redox imbalance, perturbed membrane potential, reduced growth, and increased sensitivity to antibiotics through yet-to-be-defined mechanisms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the downstream consequences of reduced cAMP.

claim: Host-associated signals like low pH can activate Mtb adenylate cyclases.
source: Moreover, it is known that host-associated signals like low pH can activate Mtb adenylate cyclases and that macrophage infection results in a burst of bacterial cAMP production (Bai et al., 2009; Tews et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2009 and Tews et al., 2005.

claim: Macrophage infection results in a burst of bacterial cAMP production.
source: Moreover, it is known that host-associated signals like low pH can activate Mtb adenylate cyclases and that macrophage infection results in a burst of bacterial cAMP production (Bai et al., 2009; Tews et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bai et al., 2009 and Tews et al., 2005.

claim: Both macE and rv1339 were recently found to be under positive selection.
source: It is interesting to note that both macE and rv1339 were recently found to be under positive selection (Liu et al., 2022), raising the possibility that alterations in cAMP levels are being positively selected in Mtb clinical isolates.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: The canonical cAMP phosphodiesterase rv0805 was not identified as a suppressor of palmitic acid toxicity in the ΔmacE suppressor screen nor in the hypoxia TnSeq screen.
source: Notably, the canonical cAMP phosphodiesterase rv0805 was not identified as a suppressor of palmitic acid toxicity in the ΔmacE suppressor screen nor in the hypoxia TnSeq screen (Rittershaus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on the suppressor screen results and cited TnSeq data.

claim: Rv0805 is 150 times more active against 2',3'-cAMP than 3',5'-cAMP.
source: Rv0805 is 150 times more active against 2',3'-cAMP, a cAMP species associated with RNA degradation, than 3',5'-cAMP, the product of adenylate cyclases (Keppetipola and Shuman, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keppetipola and Shuman, 2008.

claim: Overexpression of Rv0805 showed only a modest (~40%) reduction in 3',5'-cAMP in Mtb.
source: Consistent with these data, overexpression of Rv0805 showed only a modest (~40%) reduction in 3',5'-cAMP in Mtb (Agarwal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Agarwal et al., 2009.

claim: rv0805 has a limited phylogenetic distribution and is not found in M. smegmatis.
source: Lastly, rv0805 has a limited phylogenetic distribution and is not found in M. smegmatis, which also encodes numerous adenylate cyclases.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: rv1339 and not rv0805 is the major 3',5'-cAMP phosphodiesterase in Mtb.
source: Thus, it appears that rv1339 and not rv0805 is the major 3',5'-cAMP phosphodiesterase in Mtb (Thomson et al., 2022).
evidence: This is concluded from the collective evidence and supported by citation to Thomson et al., 2022.

claim: The adenylate cyclase Rv1625c has been shown to be important for cholesterol catabolism.
source: The adenylate cyclase Rv1625c has recently been shown to be important for cholesterol catabolism, although interestingly this phenotype was independent of the Rv1625c cyclase homology domain (Wilburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wilburn et al., 2022.

claim: V-59 is an Rv1625c agonist analogous to the eukaryotic adenylate cyclase activator forskolin.
source: In a screen for compounds that disrupt cholesterol catabolism, VanderVen and colleagues discovered V-59, an Rv1625c agonist analogous to the eukaryotic adenylate cyclase activator forskolin (VanderVen et al., 2015; Wilburn et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to VanderVen et al., 2015 and Wilburn et al., 2022.

claim: V-59 results in constitutive activation of Rv1625c and cAMP production.
source: V-59 results in constitutive activation of Rv1625c and cAMP production and, for reasons yet unknown, blocks cholesterol catabolism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to VanderVen et al., 2015 and Wilburn et al., 2022.

claim: V-59 blocks cholesterol catabolism for reasons yet unknown.
source: V-59 results in constitutive activation of Rv1625c and cAMP production and, for reasons yet unknown, blocks cholesterol catabolism.
evidence: This is stated as an unknown mechanism.

claim: Proper metabolic function of Mtb grown on fatty acids and cholesterol requires 'just the right amount' of cAMP.
source: Thus, it would appear proper metabolic function of Mtb grown on fatty acids and cholesterol requires 'just the right amount' of cAMP: too little and Mtb cannot grow in the presence of fatty acids, too much and Mtb cannot catabolize cholesterol.
evidence: This is inferred from the collective data on cAMP levels and fatty acid/cholesterol metabolism.

claim: Deficient or elevated cAMP production may potentiate combination drug therapy.
source: Moreover, our results and those investigating combination drug treatment with V-59 (Wilburn et al., 2022) suggest that deficient or elevated cAMP production may potentiate combination drug therapy.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to Wilburn et al., 2022.

claim: Large-scale chemical genomic screening of cAMP-deficient Δcya E. coli did not identify any significant differences in antibiotic susceptibility.
source: Interestingly, whereas cAMP promotes intrinsic multidrug resistance in Mtb, this relationship may not be conserved or in some cases may even be reversed in other bacteria. Large-scale chemical genomic screening of cAMP-deficient Δcya E. coli did not identify any significant differences in antibiotic susceptibility (Nichols et al., 2011), although earlier studies found that Δcya in E. coli and S. typhimurium promotes fosfomycin resistance by reducing expression of the GlpT and UhpT uptake systems (Shiver et al., 2016; Silver, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nichols et al., 2011, Shiver et al., 2016, and Silver, 2017.

claim: Δcya in E. coli and S. typhimurium promotes fosfomycin resistance by reducing expression of the GlpT and UhpT uptake systems.
source: Large-scale chemical genomic screening of cAMP-deficient Δcya E. coli did not identify any significant differences in antibiotic susceptibility (Nichols et al., 2011), although earlier studies found that Δcya in E. coli and S. typhimurium promotes fosfomycin resistance by reducing expression of the GlpT and UhpT uptake systems (Shiver et al., 2016; Silver, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shiver et al., 2016 and Silver, 2017.

claim: In uropathogenic E. coli, cAMP was found to be a negative regulator of persistence.
source: In uropathogenic E. coli, cAMP was also found to be a negative regulator of persistence (Molina-Quiroz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Molina-Quiroz et al., 2018.

claim: Δcya in uropathogenic E. coli upregulated the oxidative stress response and SOS-dependent DNA damage repair and promoted survival to beta-lactam antibiotics.
source: Δcya upregulated the oxidative stress response and SOS-dependent DNA damage repair and promoted survival to beta-lactam antibiotics.
evidence: This is based on the work cited from Molina-Quiroz et al., 2018.
